cards.explanation: It protects workers and limits onward transmission; chemical and radiation risks also need controls.
cards.text: Good microbiological practice reduces exposure to sources of {{c1::infection}}.
cards.question: Good microbiological practice reduces exposure to sources of {{c1::infection}}.

cards.explanation: Microbes can pass from fingers or contaminated objects to the mouth.
cards.text: Eating with contaminated hands can cause laboratory infection by {{c1::ingestion}}.
cards.question: Eating with contaminated hands can cause laboratory infection by {{c1::ingestion}}.

cards.explanation: Sharps can breach the protective skin barrier.
cards.text: A contaminated needlestick is a {{c1::percutaneous}} exposure.
cards.question: A contaminated needlestick is a {{c1::percutaneous}} exposure.

cards.explanation: Contaminated fingers can also transfer organisms to this mucosal surface.
cards.text: An infectious splash into the eye exposes the {{c1::conjunctiva}}.
cards.question: An infectious splash into the eye exposes the {{c1::conjunctiva}}.

cards.explanation: An aerosol may be generated without an obvious visible spill.
cards.text: Airborne laboratory aerosols create a risk of {{c1::inhalation}} exposure.
cards.question: Airborne laboratory aerosols create a risk of {{c1::inhalation}} exposure.

cards.explanation: It limits escape of the handled organism and entry of unwanted environmental organisms.
cards.text: Aseptic practice protects both the worker and the {{c1::culture}} from contamination.
cards.question: Aseptic practice protects both the worker and the {{c1::culture}} from contamination.

cards.explanation: Use approved mechanical pipetting equipment rather than risking ingestion.
cards.text: Pipetting by {{c1::mouth}} is prohibited in microbiological work.
cards.question: Pipetting by {{c1::mouth}} is prohibited in microbiological work.

cards.explanation: Gloves and laboratory coats do not replace hand hygiene.
cards.text: Before leaving a microbiology laboratory, workers should {{c1::wash their hands}}.
cards.question: Before leaving a microbiology laboratory, workers should {{c1::wash their hands}}.

cards.explanation: The safety issue is dispersal into air, not only direct contact with liquid.
cards.text: Vigorous culture handling and poorly sealed centrifuge tubes can generate infectious {{c1::aerosols}}.
cards.question: Vigorous culture handling and poorly sealed centrifuge tubes can generate infectious {{c1::aerosols}}.

cards.explanation: The source discusses HSE alongside advisory and security bodies; its historical dates are not a current legal checklist.
cards.text: The UK regulator abbreviated HSE is the {{c1::Health and Safety Executive}}.
cards.question: The UK regulator abbreviated HSE is the {{c1::Health and Safety Executive}}.

cards.explanation: It provides advice concerning biological agents and their hazards.
cards.text: ACDP stands for Advisory Committee on {{c1::Dangerous Pathogens}}.
cards.question: ACDP stands for Advisory Committee on {{c1::Dangerous Pathogens}}.

cards.explanation: Biological agents as well as hazardous chemicals can be relevant to a laboratory assessment.
cards.text: CoSHH addresses substances {{c1::hazardous to health}}.
cards.question: CoSHH addresses substances {{c1::hazardous to health}}.

cards.explanation: Workers also have responsibilities to use controls and follow safe procedures.
cards.text: Providing suitable training and fit-for-purpose safety equipment is an {{c1::employer}} responsibility.
cards.question: Providing suitable training and fit-for-purpose safety equipment is an {{c1::employer}} responsibility.

cards.explanation: The lecture includes containment, disinfection and waste disposal within this remit.
cards.text: The BSO advises on laboratory {{c1::biological safety}}.
cards.question: The BSO advises on laboratory {{c1::biological safety}}.

cards.explanation: The four-group scheme increases towards HG4.
cards.text: The lowest biological hazard group is {{c1::HG1}}.
cards.question: The lowest biological hazard group is {{c1::HG1}}.

cards.explanation: Hazard grouping describes the agent; containment describes controls applied to work.
cards.text: The highest biological hazard group is {{c1::HG4}}.
cards.question: The highest biological hazard group is {{c1::HG4}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture pairs their numbers as a teaching rule. The actual activity and risk assessment determine the required controls; a numbered group alone is not a complete operating instruction.
cards.text: A pathogen's hazard group and a laboratory's containment level describe {{c1::different things}}.
cards.question: A pathogen's hazard group and a laboratory's containment level describe {{c1::different things}}.

cards.explanation: This is a source example rather than a claim that every yeast is low hazard.
cards.text: The yeast example used for HG1 in the lecture is {{c1::Saccharomyces cerevisiae}}.
cards.question: The yeast example used for HG1 in the lecture is {{c1::Saccharomyces cerevisiae}}.

cards.explanation: Species, strain, activity and the current approved list matter when assessing real work.
cards.text: The lecture places Mycobacterium tuberculosis in {{c1::hazard group 3}}.
cards.question: The lecture places Mycobacterium tuberculosis in {{c1::hazard group 3}}.

cards.explanation: Do not generalise all viruses to one hazard group.
cards.text: Ebola virus is used as an example of {{c1::hazard group 4}}.
cards.question: Ebola virus is used as an example of {{c1::hazard group 4}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture particularly discusses containment-level 2 and 3 work; selection depends on the risk assessment.
cards.text: A microbiological safety cabinet is indicated when work creates a risk of infectious {{c1::aerosol exposure}}.
cards.question: A microbiological safety cabinet is indicated when work creates a risk of infectious {{c1::aerosol exposure}}.

cards.explanation: Correct selection and installation are also necessary; the presence of a cabinet alone is insufficient.
cards.text: A safety cabinet must be correctly used and {{c1::maintained}} to provide its intended protection.
cards.question: A safety cabinet must be correctly used and {{c1::maintained}} to provide its intended protection.

cards.explanation: It is a particle-filtration term, not proof that all gases or vapours are removed.
cards.text: HEPA means High Efficiency {{c1::Particulate Air}} filtration.
cards.question: HEPA means High Efficiency {{c1::Particulate Air}} filtration.

cards.explanation: The layout diagram emphasises keeping cabinet airflow unobstructed.
cards.text: Nearby movement can disturb the protective {{c1::airflow}} of a safety cabinet.
cards.question: Nearby movement can disturb the protective {{c1::airflow}} of a safety cabinet.

cards.explanation: The slide illustrates layered containment and clear hazard labelling. Current transport requirements must be checked separately rather than inferred from this old slide.
cards.text: An infectious specimen needs secure primary containment plus {{c1::secondary containment}}.
cards.question: An infectious specimen needs secure primary containment plus {{c1::secondary containment}}.

cards.explanation: Risk cannot be assumed unchanged merely because the starting strain was familiar.
cards.text: Genetic modification may change a microorganism's {{c1::hazard}}.
cards.question: Genetic modification may change a microorganism's {{c1::hazard}}.

cards.explanation: The source also emphasises local oversight and monitoring.
cards.text: Choosing a less hazardous host is a form of {{c1::risk reduction}} in genetic modification.
cards.question: Choosing a less hazardous host is a form of {{c1::risk reduction}} in genetic modification.

cards.explanation: These are distinct potential recipients of harm.
cards.text: A GM risk assessment considers human health, animal health and the {{c1::environment}}.
cards.question: A GM risk assessment considers human health, animal health and the {{c1::environment}}.

cards.explanation: The uploaded safety slides contain historical legal and classification statements; current procedures must use current institutional and HSE guidance.

slides.text:
Good microbiological practice & Containment #2
When handling micro-organism aseptic techniques should be used at all times.
Why?
To prevent contamination of the laboratory or personnel by the organisms being handled
To prevent contamination of the organisms from the environment or handler

slides.topic: Laboratory Safety — CoSHH, Containment & Risk — source 10
slides.text:
Aseptic techniques include: 
No mouth pipetting.
No eating, drinking, smoking or applying makeup or mobiles.
General tidiness and cleanliness: 
Cleaning up spillage with suitable agent. 
Placing used pipette in disinfectant tip down.
Clearly label all specimens.
Loops sterilised immediately after use in Bunsen flame and ensuring the loop is not overload to prevent spitting.
Wash hand before leaving the laboratory.
No open toes or soft fabric shoes.
Designated Micro lab coat and safety glass

slides.topic: Laboratory Safety — CoSHH, Containment & Risk — source 11
slides.text:
Aseptic techniques include: 
Avoid creation of aerosols:
Don’t blow material from pipettes.
Don’t shake cultures too vigorously.
Don’t expose culture to air for too long.
Care should be taken with post-mortem dissection.
Care when grinding/homogenisation tissue.
Care when centrifugation – tube should be well sealed.

slides.topic: Laboratory Safety — CoSHH, Containment & Risk — source 12
slides.text:
Current legislation 
Strict legislation for control of the handing of micro-organism.
Control by a number of government bodies: 
Health and Safety Executive (HSE) (Act 1974).
Advisory Committee on Dangerous Pathogens (ACDP). 
The National Counter Terrorism Security Office (NaCTSO).
These bodies have produced a number of reports
The Howie report – established code of practice for prevention of infection in clinical labs and post-mortem room.
Categorise pathogens according to hazard and category of containment (ACDP).
“The approved list of biological agent” last updated 2013

slides.text:
Assessment of risk
Microbial pathogens are categorised according to hazard and containment by ACDP. 
Micro organisms are categorised in one of four group:
Hazard group 1 contains micro-organisms with the lowest level of risk.
Hazard group 4 contain micro-organisms with the highest level of risk.

slides.topic: Laboratory Safety — CoSHH, Containment & Risk — source 17
slides.text:
Hazard Grouping (HG) 
Example of Hazard group 1 pathogens:
Bacteria: Bacillius subtilis, Lactobacillus casei
Yeast: Saccharomyces cerevisiae
Example of hazard group 2 microbes:
Bacteria: Escherichia coli, methicillin resistant Staphlyococcus aureus, Clostridium tetani (tetanus).
Fungi: Candida albicans (thrush), Aspergillus sp. (lung disease).
Parasite: Toxoplasma gondii (toxoplasmosis), Schistosoma mansoni (schistosomiesis).
Virus: Epstein-barr virus (glandular fever), Measles virus, Mumps virus, polio virus (vaccines existed), BCG vaccine.


http://www.hse.gov.uk/biosafety/biologagents.pdf

slides.topic: Laboratory Safety — CoSHH, Containment & Risk — source 26
slides.text:
Movement of microbes
Move of pathogen between laboratory has always been problematic. 
Regulation have been tighten since early 2000.
Regulated by  number of agencies:
Department of transport
Transport of infectious substance (2006).
ACDP, NaCTSO and HSE.
Hazard group 3 and 4 microbes must not sent through the post. 
Group 4 microbes usually have a police escort and expert used to handling the pathogen.
Group 4 microbes also require government approval before  movement.  
http://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/+/http://www.dft.gov.uk/pgr/freight/dgt1/guidance/guidancenonclass7/guidanceontransportofinfecti3186

slides.topic: Laboratory Safety — CoSHH, Containment & Risk — source 28
slides.text:
Genetic manipulation/modification organism (GMO)
Genetic make up of microbes may change naturally (antibiotic resistance) or intentionally in the laboratory.
Therefore may be necessary to up-grade their hazard group.
Regulated by  number of agencies: 
Guidance from the Scientific Advisory Committee on Genetic Modification (SACGM);
HSE. 
ADCP.
Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA).
Scottish Executive Environment and Rural Affairs Department (SSREAD).

slides.topic: Laboratory Safety — CoSHH, Containment & Risk — source 29
slides.text:
GMO #2
Within laboratory GMO is regulated by:
GM committee and the BSO.
Are subject to all regulations that affect non GMO microbiology laboratories.   
Subject to a higher level of monitoring
Health surveillance of employees to detect adverse reaction/ill health to prevent further exposure.
Choose the less hazardous microbe to manipulate.

slides.topic: Laboratory Safety — CoSHH, Containment & Risk — source 30
slides.text:
GMO #3
GM risk assessment should consider the potential impact to:	
Human health.
Animal health.
The environment.
GM risk assessment should be reviewed regularly and up date in light of new knowledge: 
These risk assessments must be kept for 10 years after the work has end.

slides.topic: Laboratory Safety — CoSHH, Containment & Risk — source 31
slides.text:
Summary 
Safe working practises in any laboratory is paramount.
Especially important in microbiology when the risk may be unknown.
It is a highly legislated by a number of bodies:
HSE, ACDP, NaCTSO, DoT, DEFRA.
Micro organism are categorised into group with HG1 being the lowest group and 4 being the highest group.
HG are manipulated at the same containment level.
